narrative: Monday, 11:44 AM. The coffee had gone cold.
James had the engagement log open. Two confirmed live hosts. He knew the next step — he had done this a dozen times in labs. Port scan. Find the open ports.
Maya glanced over. 'What state do you expect the ports to come back as?'
James paused, finger over the Enter key. 'Open or closed.'
'And what does open actually mean? Not the word. What happens on the network when a port is open?'

James thought about it. He had typed port numbers hundreds of times. Port 80 for web. Port 22 for SSH. He knew the port numbers — but he had never asked himself why those numbers existed, or what 'open' meant at the level of packets and processes.
'There's... a service listening on it?' he offered.

'Close. There is a process on the target machine registered to that port number, waiting to accept incoming connections. When your scanner sends a packet to that port, the process is there to receive it. That is what open means — something is home at that specific door, and the door is unlocked.'

'Right. The host is alive — we confirmed that in Mission 1. But on this specific port, no process is waiting. The host receives your probe — and sends back a rejection. That rejection is a real answer from a real system. The door is there, but it is locked and empty.'
'Open and closed. Okay.' James started to type again.
Maya put her hand on his arm. 'There is a third state.'

'Filtered,' she said. 'The hardest one to interpret. The one most beginners do not think about — and the one that hides the most interesting things on a real engagement.' She turned back to the screen. 'Let me show you what happens at the network level in each case.'

characters.name: Maya Patel
characters.description: Six years of experience. Maya has never run a port scan without knowing precisely what each result means — and what it does not.

characters.name: James Okafor
characters.description: Second week of his first real engagement. James knows how to use Nmap. He is learning what Nmap is actually measuring.
